To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
RAS modulation prevents progressive, cognitive impairment after experimental ischemic stroke, a finding that has important clinical implications.

RAS modulator therapy, either with an angiotensin II type 1 receptor blocker or an angiotensins II type 2 receptor agonist, prevents progressive cognitive decline after stroke, and that these protective effects can be achieved even if treatment is delayed up to 1 week.

RAS modulation, either by blocking the AT1 receptor or by stimulating the AT2 receptor, initiated after stroke in spontaneously hypertensive stroke-prone rats, reduces cognitive impairment, and that the effects are independent of β-amyloid deposition and BP.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new approach to treating cognitive impairment in patients with vascular dementia.
the effects of RAS modulation after stroke on cognitive function.
the development of new therapeutic strategies for VCID, which is a major unmet need in the aging population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our study shows that RAS modulation with either AT2R activation or AT1R blockade, after experimental stroke, prevents progressive cognitive impairment.
RAS modulation is a promising strategy to preserve cognition in patients with VCID.

the RAS modulation with C21, candesartan and C21+candesartan, initiated in the acute phase or delayed for 7 days after stroke in SHR, prevents chronic microgliosis and preserves long-term cognitive function, independent of BP or β-amyloid burden, in a clinically relevant model of stroke.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
RAS modulation is a promising approach to preventing progressive cognitive impairment after stroke and warrants further clinical investigation in humans.
the RAS is a promising therapeutic target for the treatment of cognitive impairment after stroke.
RAS modulation is a promising therapeutic strategy for VCID after stroke.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the AT2R may be the preferred RAS target for the treatment of cognitive dysfunction after stroke.
RAS modulation is an effective therapeutic strategy for the prevention and treatment of cognitive impairment in the post-stroke period, even if treatment is delayed.
the RAS is a viable target for VCID treatment, even after stroke, which has the potential to translate into clinical trials.
